economy.public_money_need.plain: The figures behind the Disaster funding and need page: for each municipio, the FEMA money of disasters and grants of 2017 to 2025 in three programs, HUD's Community Development Block Grant money (disaster and yearly grants) of federal fiscal years 2019 on, its residents, and two measures of need, so money per resident can be set next to need. It adds no source; every value comes from data files the observatory already publishes.
economy.public_money_need.definition: public_money_need.json holds, for the 78 municipios in the order of geo.ids: money.pa (FEMA Public Assistance obligated, federal share, by applicant and declaration year), money.ia (FEMA Individual Assistance approved for owners and renters, by declaration year) and money.hma (FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance federal share approved, by benefiting municipio and fiscal year), each in dollars summed over 2017 to 2025 (years.first, years.last); population (2020 Census residents); need.eal (FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss from natural hazards, $ a year; need_year.eal names its version) and need.cre3 (Census Community Resilience Estimates, % of residents with three or more risk factors, the year in need_year.cre3); and hma.approved, hma.obligated, hma.pending (dollars awaiting a FEMA decision) and hma.projects (approved subapplications). money.cdbg_dr (HUD CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT subawards by municipio of the work) and money.cdbg (HUD yearly CDBG: entitlement grants plus state program subawards), each summed over the federal fiscal years in money_years; cdbg_parts splits money.cdbg into entitlement and state and gives the island totals (entitlement_total, state_prime, state_subawards, dr_subawards). island.<program>.total is Puerto Rico's total (for HUD, the prime grants' obligations) with the money recorded as statewide and island.<program>.placed the part in the 78 municipios; hma_island holds Puerto Rico's Hazard Mitigation totals. inputs names the series each field is read from; notes.hma_payment_reported counts the subapplications with a payment reported.
economy.public_money_need.method: public_money_need.py reads economy_series.json (fema_pa_obligated, hma_approved_federal, hma_obligated, hma_pending_federal, hma_projects), housing_series.json (fema_ia_amount, population in 2020), environment_series.json (nri_eal_total) hazard_series.json (cre_risk3_pct, the latest year), spending_cdbgdr.json (cdbg_dr.py) and spending_cdbg.json (cdbg_regular.py), adds each money series over the years 2017 to 2025 (a blank year adds nothing) and checks that every file lists the 78 municipios in the same order and that no program's municipios add up to more than Puerto Rico. The page divides money by 2020 residents, ranks the 78 municipios on each measure and cuts them into thirds of 26 (a bivariate map of nine colours), and gives the rank correlation (Spearman) and the medians; it states facts and draws no conclusions. HUD's money is never added to FEMA's: it is counted by the federal fiscal year HUD obligated it.
economy.public_money_need.how_to_read: Of the FEMA Public Assistance obligated for 2017 to 2025, 22% is placed in a municipio; the rest is recorded as statewide (power, water and Commonwealth agencies), so a municipio's value leaves out statewide projects that also served it. Individual Assistance is all placed (100%), Hazard Mitigation 64%. Hazard Mitigation: $3.67 billion approved for Puerto Rico, $0.77 billion obligated and $1.06 billion awaiting a FEMA decision.
caveats: Obligated or approved money is not money spent or paid. FEMA reports a payment for 163 of 1,134 Hazard Mitigation subapplications, too few to show money paid.
Expected annual loss is a model estimate that grows with the value of what is exposed; it is not a record of losses.
The three programs follow different steps (obligated, approved), so their sum is a rough total.
A municipio can rank high on money because of one large project; a Hazard Mitigation project that benefits several municipios is split equally among them.
HUD's subawards cover only the part of the grants that the Puerto Rico Department of Housing passed on and reported with a municipio; subawards often arrive a year or more after the grant.

economy.hma_projects.plain: How many Hazard Mitigation subapplications (projects, plans and their management) FEMA approved for each municipality, by the fiscal year of the grant. A project that benefits several municipalities counts in each one.
economy.hma_projects.definition: Number of Hazard Mitigation Assistance subapplications in Puerto Rico that FEMA approved (status Approved, Closed, Completed or Subaward Accepted), by benefiting municipality and federal fiscal year. A subapplication that names several municipalities counts once in each; the Puerto Rico value counts each subapplication once.
economy.hma_projects.method: economy_series.py, functions fema_hma, hma_place and fema_values. The build pages through every OpenFEMA HmaSubapplications (v2) record whose subapplicant state is PR (1,134 downloaded on 2026-10-30). It leaves out the 5 records of fiscal years before 2000 (the price index in the file starts in 2000). Statuses Approved, Closed, Completed and Subaward Accepted count as approved; Pending and Submitted to FEMA as awaiting a decision; the 95 records with other statuses (denied, not selected, ineligible, void, withdrawn) add only their obligated money, which is zero. The benefitingCounties text is split at semicolons, and each name, without accents, capitals, apostrophes and the word 'Municipio', is matched to the 78 municipalities. A subapplication that names several municipalities is split equally among them; one that names 'Statewide', a place that is not a municipality, or nothing is kept in a statewide group. The Puerto Rico value is the 78 municipalities plus that group; its share is stored in economy_series.json under extras.statewide_share.
economy.hma_projects.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot FEMA approved 844 subapplications from fiscal year 2001 to 2025, 396 of them for fiscal year 2017 (most in San Juan: 41). A count says nothing about size: one flood-control project and one generator count the same.
caveats: The 78 municipalities add up to more than Puerto Rico when a subapplication benefits several of them, so the '% of the Puerto Rico total' option is not offered.
The year is the federal fiscal year of the grant's funding opportunity. For disaster grants (HMGP) it is the fiscal year in which the disaster was declared, so Hurricane Maria's money is under 2017.

The municipality is the one the subapplication says it benefits, not the subapplicant's location. Splitting a project that benefits several municipalities equally is the observatory's choice: the data do not say how the benefit is shared.
Hazard Mitigation Assistance is mitigation as stand-alone projects and plans. Mitigation inside Public Assistance repairs is in economy.fema_pa_406_mitigation. Do not add the two.
Payments are not published: FEMA reports a payment amount for only 163 of the 1,134 Puerto Rico subapplications (the field comes from FEMA GO only), so a sum would understate what was paid.
The Puerto Rico value includes the statewide group, so it is larger than the sum of the 78 municipalities.
OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms: name the data set (HmaSubapplications, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-30), and say the product is not endorsed by FEMA.

housing.fema_ia_amount.plain: The dollars the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) approved for households after disasters declared in a given year, by municipality. It shows aid approved, not damage and not necessarily money paid out.
housing.fema_ia_amount.definition: Sum, over the disasters declared in a calendar year, of the total approved under FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) in the municipality, for owners and renters together (OpenFEMA field totalApprovedIhpAmount). The year is the year of the disaster declaration.
housing.fema_ia_amount.method: The observatory uses the same records and matching as the household count, adding totalApprovedIhpAmount for owners and renters across the disasters of the year, rounded to whole dollars. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the 78 municipalities. No margin of error.
housing.fema_ia_amount.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island totals are $1,348,391,207 in 2017 (Irma and Maria) and $650,531,031 in 2022 (Hurricane Fiona and a severe storm with flooding and landslides). It is a total, so large municipalities show large amounts; divide by residents or households to compare places. On the Analysis tab, a shaded layer starts as dollars per resident (see 'Dollars per resident').
caveats: It measures aid approved under one FEMA program, not damage, need or money received. OpenFEMA labels the field as the total amount approved.

The amounts are totals approved to FEMA applicants (owners and renters). The observatory calls them households; the data the observatory keeps hold no household identifier, so two applicants who share a home cannot be told apart.

Amounts are as OpenFEMA records them and are not adjusted for inflation. The data hold no approval date and no price year, so an amount cannot be tied to a price year: values are totals as of the download, grouped by the year of the disaster declaration. The Analysis tab can restate them with the national Consumer Price Index (CPI-U), treating each amount as dollars of the declaration year; this is an approximation, because a national index may not match price changes in Puerto Rico.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the damage or of the payment. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on the Housing page a year without a declaration shows the most recent earlier year: 2010 shows the 2008 values, 2012 to 2016 show 2011, 2018 and 2019 show 2017, 2021 shows 2020 and 2023 to 2025 show 2022. The data file has no value for those years.
Values for 2017 and 2020 combine several declarations and cannot be split by disaster in the observatory. A declaration is listed here only because OpenFEMA holds housing assistance records under it.

A municipality with no value in a declaration year has no approved-assistance record for it in the data; that is not proof that the municipality was untouched. The earliest year in the data is 2003, and OpenFEMA's dataset page says the housing assistance data cover disasters declared from November 2002 onward, so a missing earlier year does not mean there was no aid. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 21 municipalities have values for 2003 and 2008, 34 for 2011 and 60 for 2004; 2017 and 2022 have all 78, and 2020 has 77.

Individual Assistance for households only. Other FEMA money (Public Assistance for governments, hazard mitigation), insurance payouts, Small Business Administration loans and disaster-recovery grants from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are not included.

Some of this money may also be counted in the federal award series ('Federal awards, all types'). The observatory has not reconciled the two, and they use different time bases (the year of the disaster declaration here, the date of each award transaction there). Do not add them.

On its dataset page (https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2, as of 2026-10-04), OpenFEMA states that the data are self-reported and subject to human error, that the county is inferred by the system and may be overridden by the applicant, and that the financial information comes from FEMA's internal National Emergency Management Information System (NEMIS), not its official financial systems, may differ slightly from usaspending.gov and is not intended for official federal financial reporting.

OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms. The terms ask users to name the data set (Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-02) and to state that the product is not endorsed by FEMA; the credit line under the Cite button includes that statement. Check the OpenFEMA terms before reuse.

economy.fema_pa_obligated.plain: After a disaster, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) approves money to clear debris and repair public buildings, roads and utilities. This is the federal share of that money, by municipality and by the year the disaster was declared. It is money approved. It does not show damage, need, finished repairs or spending. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 11% to 88% of each year's money is recorded as statewide. No municipality is named for that money.
economy.fema_pa_obligated.definition: Sum of the federal share obligated (OpenFEMA field federalShareObligated) for Public Assistance projects in Puerto Rico, by the project's county field and by the calendar year of the disaster declaration date, in dollars rounded to whole numbers. Public Assistance pays public bodies and some nonprofits to clear debris, protect people and repair or replace facilities such as roads, schools, power and water systems. OpenFEMA describes the county field as the applicant's location, which for Puerto Rico is a municipality name. A project whose county text does not match one of the 78 municipality names, ignoring accents, capitals and any text in parentheses, goes into a statewide group. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the 78 municipalities plus the statewide group.
economy.fema_pa_obligated.method: economy_series.py, function fema_pa and the build step after it. The build pages through every record of the OpenFEMA PublicAssistanceFundedProjectsDetails data set with state code 72 (23,052 projects when downloaded on 2026-10-30) and keeps the declaration date, the county and the federal share obligated. Each project's amount is added to its municipality and declaration year, or to the statewide group for that year if the county does not match a municipality. The Puerto Rico value for a year is the 78 municipalities plus the statewide group. Share recorded as statewide = statewide dollars / (municipality dollars + statewide dollars) x 100, rounded to 0.1 (see economy.fema_pa_statewide_share). A municipality with no project in a year is blank, not zero; a municipality with projects but no federal share obligated shows zero (Dorado in 2020). The same download also gives the eight damage-category series (economy.fema_pa_cat_a to economy.fema_pa_cat_z), which add up to this one, and the Section 406 mitigation series. The records are downloaded once for each snapshot (2026-10-30 for the 2026-10 snapshot, refreshed with python economy_series.py --fema --refresh) and kept until the data are next refreshed.
economy.fema_pa_obligated.how_to_read: Look at the Puerto Rico value and the statewide share together. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the share recorded as statewide varies by year from 11.0% to 88.3% and is above half in 4 of the 12 years (2004, 2009, 2017 and 2020); it is 80.9% for 2017. Over all years combined it is 77.9% ($30.4 billion of $39.1 billion), almost entirely because of 2017. In the same snapshot, for the 2017 declarations the Puerto Rico value is $35,606,846,160; $28,818,895,705 (80.9%) is statewide and $6.8 billion is in the 78 municipalities (San Juan $625,986,512). A municipality's value is only the part of the money that FEMA tied to an applicant in that municipality. It is not the money spent there and not the damage there. On the Analysis tab a year without a declaration shows the latest earlier year in the file (labelled 'latest at or before'), so 2018 and 2019 show the 2017 values. The year control and the small trend lines in the inspector start at 2010; earlier years are in the trend chart and in the comma-separated values (CSV) download. In the 'Public money' view with the year set to Latest, the FEMA layer shows declaration year 2024 (in the 2026-10 snapshot, a Puerto Rico value of $176.1 million, with 43 municipalities holding a value), not the 2017 hurricanes.
caveats: This is money obligated, meaning approved and made available. It is not money paid, not a measure of damage or need, and not a sign that repairs are finished.
Projects recorded as statewide cannot be placed in a municipality. The share for each declaration year is in economy.fema_pa_statewide_share.

In the data downloaded on 2026-10-30, 5,816 projects carry the county 'Statewide' and one project has no county. No other county text failed to match a municipality. OpenFEMA defines the county field as the applicant location and warns that counties may not be available for territories or for applicants without a stated headquarters location. The data do not say why each project is recorded as Statewide.

The Puerto Rico value includes the statewide part, so it is larger than the sum of the municipalities (in the 2026-10 snapshot, for the 2017 declarations, by a factor of 5.2). A Puerto Rico value per resident is not comparable with a municipality's value per resident, and the municipalities' '% of the Puerto Rico total' do not add to 100%.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the money or of the work. FEMA keeps obligating money for a disaster for years, so a year's value can still grow. The 12 years hold 20 disaster declarations (counted in the OpenFEMA download of 2026-10-30). The file keeps only the year, not the disaster number.

A year can hold several unrelated declarations. In the OpenFEMA download of 2026-10-30, the 2020 value includes the January 2020 earthquakes (declaration DR-4473, $1.11 billion) and the COVID-19 pandemic declaration (DR-4493, $154 million); the 2017 value is almost all Hurricane Maria (DR-4339, $35.57 billion of $35.61 billion). Public Assistance also pays for emergency measures, so not all of it is repair.

A blank municipality means no project was recorded for it in that declaration year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the number of municipalities with a value is 28 in 2001, 21 in 2003, 74 in 2004, 17 in 2005, 25 in 2008, 5 in 2009, 32 in 2010, 65 in 2011, 78 in 2017, 45 in 2020, 78 in 2022, 43 in 2024. A blank is not proof that a place was untouched. Dorado shows $0 for 2020: it has a project, but none with a federal share obligated. About 4% of projects (927 of 23,052 in the download of 2026-10-30) have a zero or missing federal share.
County is the applicant's location, not necessarily where the damage or the work was.

economy.fema_pa_406_mitigation.plain: When FEMA pays to repair a public facility after a disaster, it can also pay to make it stronger than before, so the next disaster does less damage. It is a cost proposed, not the federal share and not money spent.

Section 406 of the Stafford Act lets FEMA pay for cost-effective measures that protect a damaged facility from future damage as part of its repair (44 CFR 206.226(e)). Projects whose county is not one of the 78 municipalities go into a statewide group; the Puerto Rico value includes it.
economy.fema_pa_406_mitigation.method: economy_series.py, functions fema_pa and fema_values: the same download and placement as economy.fema_pa_obligated (2026-10-30), summing mitigationAmount instead of federalShareObligated.

housing.fema_ia_households.plain: The number of households FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) approved for help after disasters declared in a given year, by municipality. It counts approvals, not damage. It does not show how many homes were hurt or how much help people needed.
housing.fema_ia_households.definition: Sum, over the disasters declared in a calendar year, of the number of applicants approved for FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) in the municipality. It adds the OpenFEMA Housing Assistance data for owners and for renters (field approvedForFemaAssistance). The year is the year of the disaster declaration.
housing.fema_ia_households.method: The observatory reads the OpenFEMA API (v2) entities HousingAssistanceOwners and HousingAssistanceRenters for Puerto Rico, matches each county (the municipality) to the 78 municipalities, takes the year of each disaster from DisasterDeclarationsSummaries (declarationDate), and adds approvedForFemaAssistance for owners and renters and across the disasters of the year. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the 78 municipalities (the one 'statewide' record holds zero). No margin of error.
housing.fema_ia_households.how_to_read: Read each value as 'households approved for help after disasters declared in that year'. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island totals are 475,798 households in 2017 (Irma and Maria) and 741,313 in 2022 (Hurricane Fiona and a severe storm with flooding and landslides). This is a count, so larger municipalities show larger numbers (San Juan is highest in both years). The number of approvals and the dollars do not move together: 2022 has more approvals than 2017 but about half the dollars (see the approved amount). The data do not explain this difference.
caveats: It measures aid approved, not damage, need or the number of homes affected. Who applies and is approved depends on FEMA rules and on people's access to the process.

OpenFEMA describes the counted field as the number of FEMA applicants approved for assistance. The observatory calls them households; the data the observatory keeps hold no household identifier, so they cannot show whether two applicants share a home.

Counts are added across the disasters declared in the year. A household approved under two disasters in the same year (for example Irma and Maria in 2017) is counted once for each disaster under which it was approved.

The Analysis tab's 'Per 1,000 residents' option divides households by residents, so it is not a share of households. Do not divide by the number of households to get a share: for scale, in the 2026-10 snapshot the 2022 approvals equal about 61% of the island's 1,219,658 households in the 2018-2022 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates (95% in Orocovis), and a household approved under both declarations of a year is counted twice.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the damage or of the payment. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on the Housing page a year without a declaration shows the most recent earlier year: 2010 shows the 2008 values, 2012 to 2016 show 2011, 2018 and 2019 show 2017, 2021 shows 2020 and 2023 to 2025 show 2022. The data file has no value for those years.
Values for 2017 and 2020 combine several declarations and cannot be split by disaster in the observatory. A declaration is listed here only because OpenFEMA holds housing assistance records under it.

A municipality with no value in a declaration year has no approved-assistance record for it in the data; that is not proof that the municipality was untouched. The earliest year in the data is 2003, and OpenFEMA's dataset page says the housing assistance data cover disasters declared from November 2002 onward, so a missing earlier year does not mean there was no aid. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 21 municipalities have values for 2003 and 2008, 34 for 2011 and 60 for 2004; 2017 and 2022 have all 78, and 2020 has 77.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the municipality profile shows the sum of all years in the data (2003 to 2022) with the note 'all disasters'; households approved in more than one disaster are counted more than once.

Individual Assistance for households only. Other FEMA money (Public Assistance for governments, hazard mitigation), insurance payouts, Small Business Administration loans and disaster-recovery grants from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are not included.

On its dataset page (https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2, as of 2026-10-04), OpenFEMA states that the data are self-reported and subject to human error, that the county is inferred by the system and may be overridden by the applicant, and that the financial information comes from FEMA's internal National Emergency Management Information System (NEMIS), not its official financial systems, may differ slightly from usaspending.gov and is not intended for official federal financial reporting.

OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms. The terms ask users to name the data set (Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-02) and to state that the product is not endorsed by FEMA; the credit line under the Cite button includes that statement. Check the OpenFEMA terms before reuse.

economy.fed_awards_total.plain: Federal money promised for work or benefits in a municipality in one fiscal year (October to September). It adds contracts, grants, direct payments, loans (at their estimated cost) and other aid. It is not money spent and does not measure need. San Juan's figure can include money meant for the whole island. The Puerto Rico figure also counts awards that name no municipality.
economy.fed_awards_total.definition: Sum of the five federal award groups in this dictionary (economy.fed_contracts, economy.fed_grants, economy.fed_direct_payments, economy.fed_loans and economy.fed_other) for one place and one federal fiscal year (FY), in dollars of that year. For a municipality, each group is the amount USAspending.gov reports for prime awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over the transactions dated from 1 October of the previous calendar year to 30 September of the year shown. For contracts, grants, direct payments and other assistance the amount is the money obligated. For loans it is the estimated subsidy cost, not the amount lent (see economy.fed_loans). A group with no amount for a municipality counts as zero. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's total for the whole territory, by the same rules. It includes awards that name no municipality, so the 78 municipalities add up to less than the Puerto Rico value.
economy.fed_awards_total.method: economy_series.py, functions usaspending and last_fy, and the build step after them. For each fiscal year from 2008 and each of the five award groups, the build sends two requests to the USAspending 'spending by geography' service, both by place of performance with subawards off. The county layer, filtered to the 78 municipality codes, gives each municipality's amount. The state layer, filtered to the code PR (the postal code under which USAspending keys the territory), gives the amount for the whole territory; this is the Puerto Rico value of that group. The total adds the five group values for each place and rounds to whole dollars; it differs from the sum of the group values by at most $0.50. The Puerto Rico value is not the sum of the 78 municipalities. See economy.fed_place_of_performance for the full request, the dates and how the share that names no municipality is calculated (stored in economy_series.json under extras.fed_unplaced_share). Each year is downloaded once and kept until the data are next refreshed for a new snapshot.
economy.fed_awards_total.how_to_read: Compare municipalities per resident or as a share, not in raw dollars. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has 10.4% of the island's residents (Census 2020) and between 25.9% (FY2012) and 70.6% (FY2010) of the Puerto Rico value, or between 31.9% and 76.9% of the dollars that name a municipality. The data show that San Juan's share is high; they do not show how much of it serves other places. Also in the 2026-10 snapshot, the Puerto Rico value was $11.9 billion in FY2008, peaked at $65.2 billion in FY2021 and was $38.4 billion in FY2025. Between 3.4% (FY2011) and 24.7% (FY2024) of each year's Puerto Rico value names no municipality (the 'unplaced' share), so the 78 municipalities add up to less than the island; the share is 21.6% ($8.3 billion) in FY2025. In the same snapshot, grants hold the largest unplaced amount in 11 of the 18 years and direct payments in the other seven. Direct payments are 80% of the Puerto Rico value in FY2008 and 73% in FY2025. Grants drive the peak years: $22.3 billion in FY2020 and $35.0 billion in FY2021. A municipality's value is money recorded to its place, not what its residents received. In the same snapshot, FY2009 to FY2013 totals include $1.3 to $5.6 billion a year of other assistance, mostly recorded to Adjuntas (in FY2011, other assistance is 27% of the Puerto Rico value and Adjuntas alone is 25%; see economy.fed_other). Compare the totals without that group, or compare other years, before reading a trend.
caveats: These are obligations: amounts the federal government committed to pay. They are not outlays, which are the dollars actually paid out. Some obligated money is paid in later years and some is never paid.

The loans part of this total is the estimated cost to the government of loans and loan guarantees (subsidy cost), not the amount lent, and it can be negative (see economy.fed_loans). It is small next to the other groups: in the 2026-10 snapshot, at most 4.1% of the Puerto Rico value in any year (FY2020). The total is therefore not the sum of all federal money lent, granted and paid.

The Analysis tab's description of this dataset states that awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to San Juan. San Juan's figures can therefore include money that serves other places, and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot separate money spent in San Juan from money only recorded there.
Place of performance is what the awarding agency reports, and the observatory does not check it.

The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's total for the territory (state layer, code PR), not the sum of the 78 municipalities. It includes awards that name no municipality. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for FY2025 those awards are about $8.3 billion, or 21.6% of the all-types value: $38.4 billion for Puerto Rico against $30.1 billion in the 78 municipalities (grants $9.4 billion against $4.2 billion; direct payments $28.0 billion against $25.0 billion; contracts the same). The share for every year is in economy_series.json under extras.fed_unplaced_share and in the information window of the dataset on the Analysis tab. In the same snapshot, San Juan's FY2025 value is 36.1% of the Puerto Rico value and 46.0% of the sum of the 78 municipalities.

Because the Puerto Rico value includes unplaced awards (awards that name no municipality), a Puerto Rico value per resident is not comparable with a municipality's, and the municipalities' '% of the Puerto Rico total' add up to less than 100% (between 75.3% and 96.6% in the 2026-10 snapshot, depending on the year).
Only prime awards of the types listed in the five group entries are requested. Subawards, which are amounts a recipient passes on to others, are not included.

Dollars are those of each year, not adjusted for inflation. The Analysis tab can restate them in dollars of the latest year of the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) in the file (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot; see measures.inflation_adjustment). The observatory holds no Puerto Rico price index, so adjusted dollars are an approximation. The index in the file starts in 2000, so every federal fiscal year (FY2008 onward) is adjusted with its own year's index. The population series behind 'per resident' (see measures.per_resident) starts in 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 use the 2010 population.

The Analysis tab's year control, trend chart and small trend lines start at 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 are not shown on the map. They are in the all-years comma-separated values (CSV) download and in economy_series.json, in dollars of each year. In the inspector, a caption under each small trend line gives its length and span (for example '16 yrs · 2010–25') and, when some years have no value, how many values it holds.

The population series behind 'per resident' steps up at 2020 (about 3% for Puerto Rico) because the 2011 to 2019 estimates were not revised to the 2020 census (see methods.population_vintage_break). A per-resident change from FY2019 to FY2020 includes that step.

On the Analysis tab a federal award year is labelled with its end year: 2025 means 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025. Jobs series are calendar years, American Community Survey (ACS) income and poverty are five-year windows, and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) values are declaration years. The year control applies one number to all of them.

A negative amount is a reduction of an earlier amount (for loans, a lower estimated cost). Some groups have negative values for some places and years (see the group entries). In the 2026-10 snapshot no municipality's total is negative; the smallest is Culebra in FY2010 ($903,484).

Some jumps come from one group or one municipality, for example Adjuntas in FY2009 to FY2013 under 'other assistance' (see economy.fed_other). See the group entries before reading a change as a trend.

The 2026-10 snapshot does not include FY2026, which ended on 30 September 2026. The observatory adds a year when it treats it as complete, on 15 November, about six weeks after the year ends. USAspending can still correct earlier records, and the observatory keeps a year after one download, so an older year can differ from the live USAspending site until the data are downloaded again.
USAspending.gov states no license for these data (see the source record). Check its terms before reuse.

economy.fed_contracts.plain: A federal contract is an agreement to pay a company or agency for goods or services. This is the money the government promised for contract work in the municipality in one fiscal year (October to September). It is money promised, not money spent. It can be negative when an earlier contract amount is cut.
economy.fed_contracts.definition: Obligations for prime contract awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types A, B, C and D whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), in dollars of that year. A later change that lowers an earlier contract amount is a negative transaction, so a municipality's yearly value can be negative. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for the same award types; it also counts awards that name no municipality.
economy.fed_contracts.method: Same request as economy.fed_awards_total, with award type codes A, B, C and D (AWARD_TYPES['contracts'] in economy_series.py). The value for each municipality is the 'aggregated_amount' that the USAspending 'spending by geography' service returns at the county layer for that year; the Puerto Rico value is the amount it returns at the state layer for the code PR. The source describes these amounts as obligations by federal fiscal year. Values keep cents.
economy.fed_contracts.how_to_read: Use it to see where federal purchases are recorded, and compare places per resident. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's share of the Puerto Rico contract value runs from 18.4% (FY2021) to 64.8% (FY2023). Contracts are almost all placed in a municipality: 0.0% to 3.3% of each year's Puerto Rico contract value names no municipality. A blank cell means USAspending returned no amount for that municipality and year; the data cannot tell a missing record from no activity.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,404 municipality-year cells (78 municipalities, 18 years), 245 are blank, 27 are zero and 63 are negative.

In the same snapshot, negative values appear in every year. The largest are Caguas in FY2018 (minus $60.5 million) and Dorado in FY2023 (minus $16.9 million). They are reductions of earlier commitments, not money taken from the municipality.
In the same snapshot, the Puerto Rico value is $4.6 billion in FY2018, more than four times FY2017 ($987.6 million). The data do not show which contracts account for the rise.
Place of performance is where the awarding agency says the work is done. It is not the contractor's address. Work for the whole island can be recorded in the capital (see economy.fed_awards_total).
These are obligations (amounts the federal government committed to pay), not outlays (money actually paid out).

Dollars are those of each year, not adjusted for inflation. It is money promised, not money spent. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is the largest of the five groups in 17 of the 18 years.
economy.fed_direct_payments.definition: Obligations for prime direct payment awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types 06 and 10 whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), in dollars of that year. The Analysis tab's description of the dataset calls them federal direct payments to individuals, for example benefit programs. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for these award types; it also counts payments that name no municipality.
economy.fed_direct_payments.method: Same request as economy.fed_awards_total, with award type codes 06 and 10 (AWARD_TYPES['direct_payments'] in economy_series.py). The source describes these amounts as obligations by federal fiscal year.
economy.fed_direct_payments.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, every municipality has a positive value in every year (no blank, zero or negative cells), and the Puerto Rico value rises from $9.5 billion in FY2008 to $28.0 billion in FY2025. Do not read changes in a municipality's value across those years as changes in what its residents received.

The amount that names no municipality jumps in the same years. In the 2026-10 snapshot, USAspending's Puerto Rico total for direct payments is $11.2 billion in FY2011 and $15.8 billion in FY2012, while the 78 municipalities add up to $11.2 billion and $11.7 billion. The part that names no municipality rises from $0.5 million (0.0%) in FY2011 to $4.1 billion (26.1%) in FY2012, and is $4.5 billion in FY2013 and $5.2 billion (28.7%) in FY2016. The timing matches the fall in San Juan's share; the data do not show whether the same awards moved.

Payments of types 06 and 10 are recorded by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. The data do not say whether an agency recorded a payment by the recipient's home or by its own office.

They are money promised, not money spent. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan holds most of the grant dollars that name a municipality, and in some years more than half of the island's grant dollars name no municipality.
economy.fed_grants.definition: Obligations for prime grant awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types 02, 03, 04 and 05 whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), in dollars of that year. The Analysis tab's description of the dataset states that disaster-recovery grants and block grants are included. A later change that lowers an earlier award is a negative transaction. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for grants; it also counts grants that name no municipality.
economy.fed_grants.method: Same request as economy.fed_awards_total, with award type codes 02, 03, 04 and 05 (AWARD_TYPES['grants'] in economy_series.py). economy.fed_grants.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Puerto Rico value is $1.5 billion in FY2008, $22.3 billion in FY2020, $35.0 billion in FY2021 and $9.4 billion in FY2025. economy.fed_loans.plain: This is what the federal government expects its loans and loan guarantees to cost, for loans recorded in a municipality in one fiscal year (October to September). A loan guarantee is a promise to repay a lender if a borrower does not pay. The value is not the amount lent. economy.fed_loans.definition: For prime loan awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types 07 (direct loan) and 08 (guaranteed or insured loan) whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality: the sum, over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), of the amount that USAspending's 'spending by geography' service returns. For loans that amount is the transaction's subsidy cost, not the loan's face value. The subsidy cost is the government's estimate of what a loan will cost it over its life after repayments and expected defaults. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total of the same amount; it also counts loans that name no municipality.

economy.fed_place_of_performance.plain: USAspending records each award where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes. Awards for the whole island are often recorded in San Juan, so San Juan's figures can include money meant for other places and other municipalities' figures can be low. The Puerto Rico figure is the territory total, which also counts awards that name no municipality.
economy.fed_place_of_performance.definition: The six federal award series in the observatory (economy.fed_awards_total and its five groups) come from one USAspending.gov service, 'spending by geography', asked by place of performance. Place of performance is a field on each award record, filled in by the awarding agency. The service adds up the amounts of the award transactions dated in a period, by place. The observatory asks for each federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October of the previous calendar year to 30 September) and for five groups of award types, at two layers: by municipality (county layer) and for Puerto Rico as a whole (state layer). It then adds the groups to make the total.
economy.fed_place_of_performance.method: economy_series.py, functions usaspending, last_fy and the build step after them. Request: POST to api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/ with scope place_of_performance, geo_layer county, the 78 municipality codes (72001 to 72153) as filters, subawards false, time period from 1 October of the previous year to 30 September of the fiscal year, and the award type codes of one group. The service treats the dates as the action date of each transaction (its default; checked on 2026-10-03 by comparing the totals with and without the setting). Groups: contracts A, B, C, D; grants 02, 03, 04, 05; direct payments 06, 10; loans 07, 08; other 09, 11, -1. Search dates start on 2007-10-01, so FY2008 is the first year. The observatory treats a year as complete on 15 November (the code's last_fy, about six weeks after the year ends), and USAspending can still change it later. A municipality the service does not list for a group and year is stored as blank. The build sends the same request at the state layer (geo_layer state) with the code PR, the postal code under which USAspending keys the territory. The amount it returns is the Puerto Rico value of that group: USAspending's total for the territory, which includes awards that name no municipality. The Puerto Rico value is therefore not the sum of the 78 municipalities. The total is the sum of the five groups for each place, rounded to whole dollars. For each fiscal year the build also stores the part of the all-types Puerto Rico value that no municipality holds: (Puerto Rico value minus the sum of the 78 municipalities) divided by the Puerto Rico value, times 100, rounded to 0.1 (economy_series.json, extras.fed_unplaced_share). The Analysis tab shows these shares in the information window of every federal award series. Each year and group is downloaded once and kept until the data are next refreshed for a new snapshot.
economy.fed_place_of_performance.how_to_read: Step 1: use per resident or share values, not raw dollars. Step 2: look at the group, because the groups behave differently (in the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan holds 83.5% to 96.8% of the grant dollars that name a municipality but 27.0% to 86.2% of the direct-payment dollars that do). Step 3: for the capital, treat the number as recorded there, not spent there. San Juan holds 10.4% of the island's residents (Census 2020). In the 2026-10 snapshot it holds 25.9% to 70.6% of the all-types Puerto Rico value, depending on the year, and 31.9% to 76.9% of the dollars that name a municipality. Step 4: check the cells you quote for blank, zero or negative values. Step 5: remember that the Puerto Rico value includes awards that name no municipality; check the share that names no municipality for your year (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 3.4% to 24.7% of the all-types value). Step 6: when you cite, use the Cite button (see methods.citation). Name USAspending.gov as the source, say 'obligations by place of performance, federal fiscal year' (for loans, subsidy cost) and give the snapshot label. The USAspending data in the 2026-10 snapshot were retrieved from 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04.
caveats: Blank and zero differ. Blank means the service listed no amount for that municipality, group and year. Zero means it listed an amount of exactly zero (for example, net of reductions). Neither proves that no money reached residents.
Negative values are reductions of earlier commitments (de-obligations or lowered estimates). They are real entries in the source, not errors, but they can make a municipality's group value negative.

Only prime awards are requested, and only the award type codes listed above. Subawards are not included. A test request on 2026-10-03 for the codes F001 to F010 and for IDV_A and IDV_B returned nothing for Puerto Rico's municipalities in FY2025, so those codes add nothing to that year.

Awards that name no municipality, only Puerto Rico, are in USAspending's Puerto Rico total and so in the Puerto Rico value, but in no municipality value. In the 2026-10 snapshot that is about $8.3 billion in FY2025, 21.6% of the all-types value. By group, the share that names no municipality runs from 5.2% to 61.6% of grants (FY2014 and FY2017), 0.0% to 28.7% of direct payments (FY2011 and FY2016) and 0.0% to 3.3% of contracts. In three group-year cells the 78 municipalities add up to slightly more than the territory value: other assistance in FY2008 (by $1.6 million) and FY2014 (by $2,049), and loans in FY2016 (by $23,384). The data do not say why.
A Puerto Rico value per resident includes the money that names no municipality, so it is not comparable with a municipality's value per resident.

The Analysis tab's description of the all-types series (economy.fed_awards_total) states that awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to San Juan. San Juan's figures can therefore include money that serves other places, and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot separate money spent in San Juan from money only recorded there.
Place of performance is a different field from the recipient's address. It can differ from where the people who benefit live.

economy.fed_prog_pbra.plain: Project-Based Rental Assistance: HUD rent payments to the owners of specific rental buildings for units let to low-income households, recorded where the building is, by federal fiscal year. It is money obligated, and part of it names no municipality.
economy.fed_prog_pbra.definition: Obligations for prime awards (awards made directly to the first recipient) under assistance listing 14.195 (Section 8 Housing Assistance Payments Program (Project-Based Rental Assistance), Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)) whose place of performance is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year, in dollars of that year. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for the listing; it also counts obligations that name no municipality.
economy.fed_prog_pbra.method: economy_series.py, functions usa_programs and program_values (PROGRAMS['14.195']). For each fiscal year the build asks the USAspending 'spending by geography' service for prime awards with program_numbers [14.195], once at the county layer for the 78 municipality codes and once at the state layer for PR. Unplaced share = (Puerto Rico - sum of the 78) / Puerto Rico x 100, at least 0, rounded to 0.1, stored in economy_series.json under extras.statewide_share.fed_prog_pbra. A listing is mapped, and a year kept, only when it passes the placement rule of HANDOFF decision 69: at least 20 municipalities with money, under 40% of the placed money in San Juan and at most 50% naming no municipality. A series keeps the latest unbroken run of years that pass (kept_years). The checks, their sensitivity to the thresholds and a comparison with SSA's county tables are in docs/analysis/public-money-v2-2026-10.

economy.fac_expended.plain: Federal money that the municipio government itself spent in its fiscal year, from every federal agency, as its single audit reports it. It counts money spent, not money awarded, and only the municipio government, not other bodies in the municipio.
economy.fac_expended.definition: Federal awards expended, as defined in 2 CFR 200.502, reported in the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards of the municipio government's single audit and filed with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse: the sum of amount_expended over every award line of the audit, for the municipal fiscal year (1 July to 30 June, named by the year it ends), in dollars of that year. Awards received directly from a federal agency and through a pass-through entity both count; a loan counts the amount used in the year (2 CFR 200.502(b)).
economy.fac_expended.method: economy_series.py, functions fac_audits, fac_awards and fac_values (FAC_AGENCIES). The build reads the list of Puerto Rico audits from the FAC API (general, auditee_state PR, most recent submissions, no contact fields), keeps those of the 78 municipio governments (fac_municipio: name patterns such as 'MUNICIPALITY OF', 'MUNICIPIO DE' and 'AUTONOMOUS MUNICIPALITY OF', leaving out housing projects and other bodies named after a municipio; a typo'd name is taken by an EIN that belongs to one municipio only), then reads their award lines (federal_awards) once per fiscal year and sums amount_expended. The award lines of every audit add up to its reported total. Puerto Rico = the sum of the municipios that filed; notes.fac_filed in economy_series.json counts them. The API needs an api.data.gov key (FAC_API_KEY, HANDOFF decision 70). Checks: docs/analysis/public-money-v2-2026-10/fac_check.py.
economy.fac_expended.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot (Federal Audit Clearinghouse, retrieved 2026-10-31), the 65 municipio governments that had filed for FY2025 report $1.50 billion; for FY2016, all 78 filed and report $587.5 million. In FY2025 the largest are San Juan ($169.5 million), Bayamón ($88.9 million), Ponce ($81.1 million). 65 of the 65 that filed have a value above zero. Compare municipios per resident, and compare years only where the same municipios filed.
caveats: Only the municipio government. Federal money spent in the municipio by Commonwealth agencies, nonprofits, universities, Head Start consortia and the municipio's own housing projects (which file their own audits) is not counted. Audits whose names mention a municipio but are not its government's are left out: housing projects, a community San Juan runs, Bayamón's Ryan White program filed apart, municipal alliances, a cooperative and Commonwealth offices (25 names, listed in docs/analysis/public-money-v2-2026-10/fac_check.json).

Cross-checks in docs/analysis/public-money-v2-2026-10: the municipio governments' Head Start spending, FY2019 to FY2024, follows USAspending's Head Start money by municipio (correlation 0.849; $1.33 billion against $1.50 billion, which also counts nonprofit grantees). Their FEMA Public Assistance spending in all audits is $1.54 billion, against $8.65 billion OpenFEMA shows obligated to them as applicants (a median municipio has spent 21% of it); spent and obligated measure different things.

A year is blank where the audit is not filed: a government that spent less than $750,000 of federal money in the year files none ($1,000,000 for fiscal years that start on or after 1 October 2024, so from FY2026 for the municipios; 2 CFR 200.501), and late audits are common. Not filed in the 2026-10 snapshot: FY2017 Culebra, Lares, Loíza, Moca; FY2018 to FY2019 Culebra; FY2020 Culebra, Lares; FY2023 Villalba; FY2024 Camuy, Guánica, Villalba; FY2025 Adjuntas, Camuy, Ceiba, Ciales, Comerío, Guánica, Guayanilla, Lajas, Las Marías, Las Piedras, Loíza, Morovis, Villalba. FY2016, FY2021 and FY2022 are complete. The Puerto Rico value adds up the municipios that filed, so it is low in years with missing audits, most of all FY2025; refresh the data as audits arrive (they are due nine months after the fiscal year ends).
In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 780 municipio-year cells (10 years, 78 municipios), 25 are blank (no audit filed) and 0 are zero (an audit with no money of this kind).

Money spent (expended) in the municipio's fiscal year, as the audit reports it. It is not the same as money obligated or awarded (the USAspending series) or approved (the FEMA series), and a large award can be spent over several years.

Municipal fiscal years run from 1 July to 30 June and are named by the year they end: FY2024 is July 2023 to June 2024. Federal fiscal years (October to September) are used by the USAspending series, so the two do not line up exactly.

Matched by name: the auditee names were matched to the 78 municipios, and two with typos in their names were matched by their EIN (employer identification number). One municipio filed two identical audits for FY2024; one is kept.
Values are in dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation.

The build reads the list of Puerto Rico audits from the FAC API (general, auditee_state PR, most recent submissions, no contact fields), keeps those of the 78 municipio governments (fac_municipio: name patterns such as 'MUNICIPALITY OF', 'MUNICIPIO DE' and 'AUTONOMOUS MUNICIPALITY OF', leaving out housing projects and other bodies named after a municipio; a typo'd name is taken by an EIN that belongs to one municipio only), then reads their award lines (federal_awards) once per fiscal year and sums amount_expended. The award lines of every audit add up to its reported total. Puerto Rico = the sum of the municipios that filed; notes.fac_filed in economy_series.json counts them. The API needs an api.data.gov key (FAC_API_KEY, HANDOFF decision 70). Checks: docs/analysis/public-money-v2-2026-10/fac_check.py.
economy.fac_treasury.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot (Federal Audit Clearinghouse, retrieved 2026-10-31), the 65 municipio governments that had filed for FY2025 report $296.1 million (19.7% of fac_expended); for FY2016, all 78 filed and report $0. In FY2025 the largest are San Juan ($33.2 million), Ponce ($27.1 million), Arecibo ($19.4 million). 64 of the 65 that filed have a value above zero. Compare municipios per resident, and compare years only where the same municipios filed.
caveats: Only the municipio government. Federal money spent in the municipio by Commonwealth agencies, nonprofits, universities, Head Start consortia and the municipio's own housing projects (which file their own audits) is not counted. Audits whose names mention a municipio but are not its government's are left out: housing projects, a community San Juan runs, Bayamón's Ryan White program filed apart, municipal alliances, a cooperative and Commonwealth offices (25 names, listed in docs/analysis/public-money-v2-2026-10/fac_check.json).
The five agency series (economy.fac_hhs, fac_hud, fac_dhs, fac_treasury, fac_other) add up to economy.fac_expended. Do not add one to economy.fac_expended, which already includes it.

A year is blank where the audit is not filed: a government that spent less than $750,000 of federal money in the year files none ($1,000,000 for fiscal years that start on or after 1 October 2024, so from FY2026 for the municipios; 2 CFR 200.501), and late audits are common. Not filed in the 2026-10 snapshot: FY2017 Culebra, Lares, Loíza, Moca; FY2018 to FY2019 Culebra; FY2020 Culebra, Lares; FY2023 Villalba; FY2024 Camuy, Guánica, Villalba; FY2025 Adjuntas, Camuy, Ceiba, Ciales, Comerío, Guánica, Guayanilla, Lajas, Las Marías, Las Piedras, Loíza, Morovis, Villalba. FY2016, FY2021 and FY2022 are complete. The Puerto Rico value adds up the municipios that filed, so it is low in years with missing audits, most of all FY2025; refresh the data as audits arrive (they are due nine months after the fiscal year ends).
In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 780 municipio-year cells (10 years, 78 municipios), 25 are blank (no audit filed) and 362 are zero (an audit with no money of this kind).

Money spent (expended) in the municipio's fiscal year, as the audit reports it. It is not the same as money obligated or awarded (the USAspending series) or approved (the FEMA series), and a large award can be spent over several years.

Municipal fiscal years run from 1 July to 30 June and are named by the year they end: FY2024 is July 2023 to June 2024. Federal fiscal years (October to September) are used by the USAspending series, so the two do not line up exactly.

Matched by name: the auditee names were matched to the 78 municipios, and two with typos in their names were matched by their EIN (employer identification number). One municipio filed two identical audits for FY2024; one is kept.
Values are in dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation.
These series are about federal grant money. Their Spanish summaries are held for Finance and Compliance review (HANDOFF decision 21).
economy.fac_treasury.geography: 78 municipio governments and Puerto Rico (the sum of the municipios that filed)
economy.fac_treasury.source_detail: Federal Audit Clearinghouse API (api.fac.gov), tables general and federal_awards, auditee_state PR, municipal fiscal years 2016 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-31.

economy.nmtc_qlici.plain: Dollars invested in businesses and real estate projects in low-income census tracts with New Markets Tax Credits, by the year each investment was made.
economy.nmtc_qlici.definition: The sum of the qualified low-income community investments (QLICIs: loans to, or equity in, a business or project) that Community Development Entities made with New Markets Tax Credit allocations in the municipio, by the calendar year of origination, as the CDFI Fund publishes them.
economy.nmtc_qlici.method: economy_series.py, function nmtc_values. The build reads the newest NMTC data file listed on the CDFI Fund's data releases page (cache/economy/nmtc), takes the sheet of financial notes (one row per QLICI), keeps the Puerto Rico rows and places each in the municipio of its 2020 census tract (the first five digits). 73 investments in 36 projects. Puerto Rico = the sum of the municipios.
economy.nmtc_qlici.how_to_read: From 2001 to 2023, $219.3 million of NMTC investments reached 23 municipios: San Juan $37.6 million, Manatí $32.5 million, Ponce $25.4 million. Read several years together: one project can be a large share of a year.
caveats: Each investment counts in the municipio of its own census tract; a project with investments in several municipios is counted once, in the municipio of the first one the file lists (none in Puerto Rico does in the 2026-08 release).
Investments, not the credit: investors claim 39% of each investment as a tax credit over seven years (5% a year for three years, then 6% a year for four).
Values are in dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation. Most years have no investment in Puerto Rico; 2018 has the most.
These are about a federal tax credit program. Their Spanish summaries are held for Finance and Compliance review (HANDOFF decision 21).
economy.nmtc_qlici.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the sum of the municipios)
economy.nmtc_qlici.source_detail: CDFI Fund, NMTC public data release (NMTC_Public_Data_Release_includes_FY2003_FY_2023_Data_Final_08062026.xlsx), sheet Financial Notes, QLICI Amount

economy.nmtc_projects.plain: How many projects received their first New Markets Tax Credit investment each year, in the municipio of the project.
economy.nmtc_projects.definition: The number of NMTC projects whose earliest QLICI was made that calendar year, counted in the municipio of the project's census tract.
economy.nmtc_projects.method: economy_series.py, function nmtc_values. The build reads the newest NMTC data file listed on the CDFI Fund's data releases page (cache/economy/nmtc), takes the sheet of financial notes (one row per QLICI), keeps the Puerto Rico rows and places each in the municipio of its 2020 census tract (the first five digits). 73 investments in 36 projects. Puerto Rico = the sum of the municipios. A project counts once, in the year of its first investment.
economy.nmtc_projects.how_to_read: From 2001 to 2023, 36 projects in Puerto Rico received NMTC investments. Most years have none or a handful, so add years together before comparing municipios.
caveats: Each investment counts in the municipio of its own census tract; a project with investments in several municipios is counted once, in the municipio of the first one the file lists (none in Puerto Rico does in the 2026-08 release).
Values are in dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation. Most years have no investment in Puerto Rico; 2018 has the most.

economy.spending_pica.plain: Where the government plans to build: the capital improvements the Planning Board recommends for the next four fiscal years, by municipio and agency. It covers the agencies and public corporations in the program, including the Aqueduct and Sewer Authority, the Highways and Transportation Authority, the Department of Education and the University of Puerto Rico. A plan, not money already approved or spent.
economy.spending_pica.definition: spending_pica.json holds the adopted Four-Year Investment Program (Programa de Inversiones de Cuatro Años, PICA) of the Junta de Planificación, read project line by project line: by_muni gives the dollars of each fiscal year (years, July to June, named by the year it ends) for each of the 78 municipios (geo.ids); by_agency gives each agency's dollars per municipio over the four years and its dollars not placed in a municipio; unplaced gives, for each year, the dollars of lines that name several municipios as a region, the whole island or no place. population is the Census Bureau's estimate for July 1 2025, for per-resident figures. total_usd is the sum of the lines read, stated_total_usd the program's own total and gap_usd the difference.
economy.spending_pica.method: pica.py finds the adopted program on jp.pr.gov, reads the PDF with pdftotext and takes every line of the agency tables whose four fiscal years add up to its total, in thousands of dollars. The municipio is the name written right before the type of project; a line that lists several municipios is split equally among them; a line for a region, several municipios without names, the whole island or no defined place is not placed. In the 2025-2026 to 2028-2029 program the lines read add up to $11.86 billion of the $11.89 billion the program states; the rest are lines the text does not lay out in full and one agency with no table (the Península de Cantera company, $4.2 million).
economy.spending_pica.how_to_read: Per resident, a few municipios stand out because one large project (a water treatment plant, a hospital) falls in them; the map shows where projects are planned, not who benefits, since a regional plant serves several municipios.
economy.spending_pica.geography: The 78 municipalities; dollars not placed in a municipio separately

economy.spending_state.plain: What the Government of Puerto Rico's agencies spent in recent fiscal years, what the Legislature approved and what the governor proposed, split by agency, by the fund the money comes from (general, special or federal), by what it pays for (payroll, purchased services, transfers, capital works, debt service, other) and by function (education, health, public safety and so on). It is island-wide: the budget does not say in which municipio the money is spent.
economy.spending_state.definition: spending_state.json holds, for the agencies in the fiscal plan, one row for each agency (three-digit OGP code, named in agencies), fund (funds: general = Fondo General, special = Fondos Especiales, federal = Fondos Federales), concept of expense (concepts) and function (functions) that has money, with its whole dollars in each of the columns. A column is a fiscal year (July to June, named by the year it ends) and a stage: actual (OGP's 'Gastado'), approved ('Aprobado') or proposed (the governor's last 'Propuesto'). Each column names the data sheet it comes from and OGP's own total for it (stated_total); total is the sum of the rows. notes say which columns of other sheets were not used and why.
economy.spending_state.method: ogp_budget.py reads every OGP data sheet (Sábana) linked from www.presupuestos.pr.gov: one line per agency, fund, program, concept and object of expense, in thousands of dollars. Each fiscal year and stage comes from the newest sheet whose lines add up to its stated total within 0.5% (the FY27 approved sheet leaves out lines with no FY27 money, so its FY25 and FY26 columns are not used; a draft marked Privileged & Confidential is not read). Each line's function and concept come from the function crosswalk (dictionary_src/spending_crosswalk.csv): debt amortization and pensions are debt_pensions whatever the agency, a few programs and objects of the custodial accounts have their own function, and every other line takes its agency's. The lines are added up by agency, fund, concept and function.
economy.spending_state.how_to_read: Compare an approved column with the actual one of the same year to see how far spending ran from the budget, and the proposed with the approved to see what the Legislature changed. Never add two columns: they are different stages, or different years, of the same money.
economy.spending_state.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (the budget names no municipio)

economy.spending_cdbgdr.plain: Where the federal disaster recovery and mitigation money that the Puerto Rico Department of Housing manages was passed on, as subawards to municipalities, contractors and nonprofits, by the municipio where the work is reported, in each federal fiscal year. It covers only the reported subawards, not the money the Department spends through its own programs.
economy.spending_cdbgdr.definition: spending_cdbgdr.json holds, for each federal fiscal year (October to September), the first-tier subawards that USAspending.gov reports under the Puerto Rico Department of Housing's disaster grants (assistance listing 14.228; the grant numbers are in awards), summed by the municipio of the place of performance (by_muni), the subawards for Puerto Rico that name no municipio (unplaced), the subawards' total (subawards) and the prime grants' obligations (prime), in dollars. grants lists each prime grant with its obligation over its life and its outlays to date (what the Treasury has paid the Department), read on grants_read.
economy.spending_cdbgdr.method: cdbg_dr.py asks USAspending.gov's API (spending_by_geography) for each final federal fiscal year, filtered to the Department of Housing's disaster grant numbers: subawards by municipio, subawards for Puerto Rico as a whole and the prime grants for Puerto Rico as a whole. The yearly block grants and the COVID grant are left out.
economy.spending_cdbgdr.how_to_read: Compare municipios per resident over the same years. Read the subawards next to the prime grants: they are the part of the money that is placed, not all of it.
economy.spending_cdbgdr.geography: Municipio, with the subawards that name no municipio apart

economy.taken_back.plain: How much the federal government lowered, for good, the money it had committed to grants for work in Puerto Rico since federal fiscal year 2019, by federal agency and by program. The data do not say why an amount was lowered: an administrative adjustment, an adjustment to actual cost, a federal cancellation or money not committed in time all look the same.
economy.taken_back.definition: taken_back.json holds, for the grants with place of performance Puerto Rico that have a transaction in USAspending.gov from federal fiscal year 2019, the count and the dollars of the grants whose obligation ended the period below the highest level it reached in the period (the net reduction), by awarding federal agency, by assistance listing and by the fiscal year of the grant's last reduction. Programs paid by actual cost, highway projects and disaster programs are kept apart.
economy.taken_back.method: taken_back.py asks USAspending.gov's transaction search for every transaction on grants (award types 02 to 05) with place of performance Puerto Rico, quarter by quarter from federal fiscal year 2019. A reduction matched by an equal increase on another grant of the same listing and agency within 31 days is a move and is left out. For each grant the transactions of one day are added, and the net reduction is the highest cumulative level reached in the period, counted from where the grant stood when the period began, minus the final level. Grants with a net reduction under $1,000 are left out. A grant that carries several listings is placed under the one with most money.
economy.taken_back.how_to_read: Read the number of grants next to the dollars: one large grant can put a program near the top. The latest fiscal years can still change, because a grant lowered this year can be raised again.
economy.taken_back.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (place of performance Puerto Rico)
